newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish pension funds continue upward climb - survey.
newsitem.headline: Irish pension funds continue upward climb - survey.

text.p: Irish pension funds continued to reap the benefits of strong equity returns in the first quarter of 1997, while Irish bonds displayed a more subdued out-turn, a survey compiled by Actuaries and Benefit Consultants, Mercer Ltd showed on Tuesday.
The average fund returned 6.7 percent in the quarter despite a retreat in March caused by an increase in U.S. interest rates, Mercer said.

"The domestic equity market continued its very strong performance of recent years, posting a gain of 11 percnet in the first quarter," Mercer's Deborah Reidy said, adding that the Irish bond index posted 0.5 percent for the quarter.
ESB Fund Managers were the top performer with 8.9 percent return, followed by Montgomery Govett who generated an 8.0 percent return.
the ESB fund managers also claimed the top position over a three year period to end March showing a 16.5 percent outturn with Eagle Star generating 15.9 percent.
The average fund registered 12.8 percent per annum over the three year period giving a real return in excess of 10 percent.
Canada Life and Standard Life shared top position over a five year period returning 15.2 percent, while New Ireland generated a return of 12.8 percent over 10 years.
The quarter's return was boosted by a strong performance from the Irish equity market combined with a robust performance in continental Europe, Mercer said.

The findings showed the UK, U.S. and Pacific Basin markets all performing well during the first two months of 1997 but retreating in March when the Federal Reserve announced an increase in interest rates as a pre-emptive strike against inflation.

"The opening two months of the year saw the market build on the strong rise of 1996. In particular, Bank of Ireland, Waterford Wedgwood, DCC and Irish Life were among the strongest performers," Mercer said.
It said the atmosphere soured in March, amid concerns of a rise in U.S. interest rates coupled with growing doubts about the feasibility of the EMU timetable.
The Irish bond market also began the year brightly, the survey showed, but later lost most of its early gains on concerns over the EMU timetable and U.S. interest rate changes.
In Wall Street, the market suffered a sharp contraction in March but still managed to hold onto much of its gains returning 9.6 percent for the quarter as a whole, Mercer said.

The UK equity market rose strongly in the first quarter on the back of continued steady growth. This performance was further enhanced for the Irish investor by the continued sterling strength, giving a total return of 8.4 percent.

Continental Europe was the star performer in the first three months of 1997, rising by 14.6 percent, the survey showed, while Japan dropped of 5.4 percent in Irish pound terms and the Pacific Basin returned 2.6 percent to the Irish investor, Mercer said.
